source: Cheng et al. (2026, v3) Revisiting Chain-of-Thought Prompting: Zero-shot Can Be Stronger than Few-shot
finding: For strong instruction-tuned models (Qwen2.5 family, Llama-3.3-70B), 8 CoT exemplars do not beat zero-shot CoT once the answer extractor is fixed. Exemplars mostly teach the output format. Masking exemplar content step by step (Replace_Q, Replace_QA, Replace_All) removes the gain; with all content masked the result falls back to zero-shot.
numbers: Qwen2.5-72B-Instruct, full test sets. GSM8K: 8-shot 95.75, zero-shot as first scored 91.58, zero-shot with boxed-answer extraction fix 95.83. MATH: 8-shot 81.30, zero-shot 81.64. Qwen2.5-72B-Base: GSM8K 8-shot 90.52, zero-shot 84.69, fixed 90.27; MATH 75.82 vs 70.60 (base models still gain).
quote: adding traditional CoT exemplars does not improve reasoning performance compared to Zero-Shot CoT. Instead, their primary function is to align the output format
limits: Instruction-tuned open models, greedy decoding, no confidence intervals, only GSM8K and MATH (near ceiling for 72B). Authors define 'strong' as zero-shot CoT >= few-shot CoT, which is circular. Not a reasoning-model test.
agent_relevance: Answers gap 1: for a strong model, a stored worked example buys format alignment, not procedure. Measure example-first against zero-shot with a fixed answer extractor, or the gain is an evaluation artifact.

source: Cheng et al. (2026) Revisiting CoT Prompting (retrieval, R1-written exemplars, OOD)
finding: Eight retrieved exemplars (TopK, Fast-Votek, DPP, MMR, EXPLORA, Complexity, Random) mostly fall below zero-shot on MATH. On GSM8K the best retrieval variant beats zero-shot by about 0.2 points, which the authors call variance. Exemplars written by DeepSeek-R1 or Qwen2.5-Max also did not help. Models attend little to exemplars. A few weak models (for example Llama3.1-8B at 8-shot) gain marginally. On LSAT, adding exemplars caused a severe drop.
numbers: Varying shots 2 to 8 on Qwen2.5-7B and 72B: zero-shot highest in most settings; complexity retrieval at 4 or 6 shots about +0.2 on GSM8K. About 100 of 1,319 GSM8K outputs were truncated or repeated and were hand-checked.
limits: Most numbers are read from figures in the text; only Table 1 has exact cells. Instruction-tuned models only. Gains for the smallest models are described but not tabulated in the text I read.
agent_relevance: Supports a rule: gate the library by model strength. Retrieval of worked examples is a weak-model tool; for a strong solver it must prove itself against zero-shot at equal tokens.

source: DeepSeek-AI (2025/2026) DeepSeek-R1: Incentivizing Reasoning Capability via RL (prompting note)
finding: The authors report that R1 is prompt-sensitive and that few-shot prompting consistently lowers its accuracy. They recommend zero-shot with the output format described. They used few-shot long-CoT prompting only to build cold-start training data.
numbers: No numbers for the few-shot drop in the text I read (one sentence in the limitations section).
quote: Few-shot prompting consistently degrades its performance. Therefore, we recommend users directly describe the problem and specify the output format using a zero-shot setting
limits: One unquantified sentence; no benchmark table, no exemplar type stated. Cannot say if worked solutions in a different style would behave the same.
agent_relevance: For reasoning-trained models the expertise-reversal analogue is plausible: the model already has its own procedure and a foreign example disturbs it. Strong prior for an A/B gate, not proof.

source: Zhao, Li, Kong (2023) Decomposing the Enigma: Subgoal-based Demonstration Learning for Formal Theorem Proving
finding: Rewriting each demonstration proof as a numbered list of subgoals (then refining the subgoals) raises Isabelle proof pass rate on miniF2F over the prior best method that used human informal proofs (DSP with Minerva 540B). Proofs are checked by the Isabelle prover, so success is code-verified.
numbers: miniF2F-test pass rate: DSP 38.9%, subgoal demos with diffusion-chosen demo set 45.5% (valid 48.0% vs 42.6%). Abstract: 38.9% to 44.3% from subgoals alone. 244 test problems; gpt-3.5-turbo-0301; 61 demonstration examples; results averaged over three runs.
limits: Formal Isabelle sketches, not natural-language maths. Subgoals are model-refined, not human-labelled as in Margulieux. The diffusion model for demo choice is trained on miniF2F-valid proofs (cumulative pass rate flagged for valid). Single benchmark.
agent_relevance: Closest LLM analogue of the subgoal-label effect, and it uses a hard verifier. Supports storing library entries as explicit subgoal lists.

source: Zhao et al. (2023) Subgoal-based demonstration learning: ablation (Table 2)
finding: Removing subgoal-based proofs lowers pass rate even when the diffusion demo organisation is kept, and removing both is worst. The gain from subgoals is similar with and without the organiser.
numbers: miniF2F-test: full 45.5; minus subgoal 40.6 (-4.9); minus diffusion 44.3; minus both 38.5. So the subgoal effect is +4.9 with organiser and +5.8 without (44.3 vs 38.5). miniF2F-valid: 48.0 / 44.3 / 47.5 / 41.8. Reaches the old best of 38.5% with 20 LLM calls per problem instead of 100.
limits: Average of three runs, no CIs. 'Minus subgoal' reverts to informal-proof demonstrations, so subgoal format and subgoal content are confounded.
agent_relevance: Answers gap 4 for an LLM: labelled-subgoal demos beat unlabelled ones by about 5 points on a verified task. Plan the same ablation in the library.

source: Madaan and Yazdanbakhsh (2022) Text and Patterns: For Effective Chain of Thought It Takes Two to Tango
finding: Counterfactual prompts alter one part of the CoT exemplar. Symbols (numbers) can be swapped for abstract placeholders or out-of-distribution values with little loss, but deleting them removes the CoT gain. Patterns (equations or structure) must be present: no-pattern or pattern-only prompts fall to near the direct-answer level. Text (natural-language glue) matters in proportion to how much it is altered.
numbers: PaLM-62B GSM8K: direct 10.11%, CoT 27.37%; wrong equations (for example 5+3=7) still 24.39%. Also reports tolerance to wrong patterns on DATE (44.84%) and SORTING (64.80%), but not on SPORTS. A concise CoT with 20%+ fewer tokens matched full CoT.
limits: Older models (PaLM, GPT-3, Codex), four tasks. Several Table 3 cells are scrambled in the PDF text, so only sentence-level numbers are used here.
agent_relevance: Answers gap 9 for maths: the gain comes from the structure and form of the steps plus readable text, not from correct numbers. A stored example needs a clear step pattern; content correctness matters less for prompting (but not for training).

source: Madaan and Yazdanbakhsh (2022) Text and Patterns: conclusion on what examples teach
finding: The authors conclude intermediate steps mainly show the model which symbols to copy into the answer, not how to solve. Together with Wang 2023 (invalid steps keep about 81% of accuracy) this explains why format and distribution can carry most of the in-context gain.
numbers: Abstract-level claim; attention analysis shows near-identical attention for original and abstract-symbol prompts.
quote: the primary role of intermediate steps may not be to facilitate learning "how" to solve a task
limits: Strong claim from one family of models in 2022. Cheng 2026 (d01) agrees for modern models; Fu 2022 and Zhou 2022 show systematically wrong content does hurt.
agent_relevance: Do not assume a stored worked example teaches the procedure. Test it against a format-only stub (same layout, masked content).

source: Toshniwal et al. (2024) OpenMathInstruct-1: A 1.8 Million Math Instruction Tuning Dataset (coverage numbers)
finding: Solutions are accepted when code execution gives the gold answer. Showing the model the reference text solution in the prompt raises accepted-solution coverage but invites shortcut solutions that copy the answer (print(ANSWER)). Masking the numbers in the shown text solution removes the shortcut and still raises coverage.
numbers: Training-set coverage MATH: 80.1% to 85.9% (single masked prompt) and 87.5% (subject-specific masked prompts); GSM8K 99.1% to 99.9%. Final data: 787K unique solutions for 6,978 of 7,500 MATH problems, 1.04M for 7,469 of 7,473 GSM8K. Fine-tuned OpenMath-CodeLlama-70B 84.6% GSM8K, 50.7% MATH.
limits: Answer-match filtering, not full reasoning verification. No rate is given for what fraction of raw generations fail; coverage is per problem after many samples (up to 128 per GSM8K problem).
agent_relevance: Answers gap 10 in part: code execution plus answer match admits cheating solutions when the worked solution leaks the answer. Library admission should run on a masked or held-out version of the problem.

source: Toshniwal et al. (2024) OpenMathInstruct-1: right answer, flawed reasoning
finding: The authors state that solutions reaching the right answer through flawed reasoning are hard to filter with syntactic rules and call them anecdotally rare. They suggest a stronger model as grader as future work. Post-processing removed multiple boxed blocks, unclosed code blocks and trailing text.
numbers: Appendix gives one example each of the copy-from-reference shortcut (Figure 11), trailing text (Figure 12) and right-answer-wrong-reasoning (Figure 13). No error rate measured.
quote: filtering semantically noisy, i.e., solutions that get to the right answer with flawed reasoning [12], is a much harder problem
limits: Qualitative. No measurement of how admitting only verified solutions changes downstream accuracy versus admitting all.
agent_relevance: A code check proves the answer, not the explanation. For an example library, add a second check (re-derive from the stored subgoals) before admission.

source: Zhang, Zhang, Li, Smola (2022) Automatic Chain of Thought Prompting (Auto-CoT): misleading by similarity
finding: When demonstrations are written by the model itself (Zero-Shot-CoT) and chosen by similarity to the test question, wrong demonstrations mislead the model into repeating the same mistake. With human-annotated chains the same retrieval works better than manual.
numbers: MultiArith: Zero-Shot-CoT gave wrong answers on 128 of 600 questions (21.3%). With annotated chains (MultiArith / GSM8K / AQuA): Manual-CoT 91.7 / 46.9 / 35.8; Random-Q-CoT 86.2 / 47.6 / 36.2; Retrieval-Q-CoT 82.8 / 48.0 / 39.7 (read from a garbled table; check before quoting).
limits: GPT-3 text-davinci-002, 2022. The row assignment in the extracted table is uncertain. Retrieval-Q-CoT with self-made chains is the failing case, not retrieval itself.
agent_relevance: Answers gap 6 partly: self-generated exemplars hurt exactly when unverified wrong chains are retrieved by similarity. A verifier that drops wrong chains removes that failure mechanism.

source: Zhang et al. (2022) Auto-CoT: effect of wrong demonstrations (Section 5.5)
finding: Diversity-based sampling (cluster, then one demo per cluster) tolerates wrong demonstrations; in-cluster similarity sampling does not. Auto-CoT accuracy does not degrade significantly even with 50% wrong demos on MultiArith.
numbers: MultiArith, wrong-demo share up to 50%; exact curve values only in Figure 6 (not extracted).
agent_relevance: If verification cannot be perfect, choose library demos for diversity, not just nearest similarity.

source: An et al. (2024) Learning From Mistakes Makes LLM Better Reasoner (LEMA)
finding: Fine-tuning on (wrong attempt, mistake step, explanation, correct answer) records written by GPT-4 beats fine-tuning on correct solutions alone, across five backbones. This is attempt-then-correction as a training signal, a loose analogue of productive failure. It is fine-tuning, not prompting.
numbers: LLaMA-2-70B: GSM8K 81.4 to 83.5 (+2.1), MATH 23.6 to 25.0 (+1.4), SVAMP +1.3, ASDiv +1.5, CSQA 84.2 to 85.3. LLaMA-65B GSM8K 76.2 to 77.9. CodeLLaMA-34B GSM8K 68.8 to 71.7. MATH to 29.3 with correction-centric evolution. A same-token (5.8M) comparison still favours LEMA.
limits: Needs GPT-4 as corrector, so teacher quality is a confound. Gains are 1 to 3 points; best checkpoint reported. Not an in-context test of example-first vs attempt-first.
agent_relevance: No study found that compares example-first and attempt-first prompts for an LLM (gap 2 stays open). LEMA only shows that failure plus correction is a useful stored item.

source: Liu, Li, Dubrawski (2026) Notes to Self: Can LLMs Benefit from Experiential Abstractions? (Table 1)
finding: A library of strategy and caution notes distilled from MATH training traces and retrieved at inference helps Llama-3.2-3B but slightly hurts Qwen-2.5-1.5B. Self-extracted notes match teacher-extracted ones. This re-opens and confirms the numbers carried from c14.
numbers: MATH-500 pass@1/pass@8: Llama baseline 43.11/70.57, inference notes 46.42/72.80, GRPO 46.89/70.54, GRPO with notes in training only 49.45/71.98, notes in train and test 47.65/70.23. Qwen baseline 50.23/76.47, inference notes 49.14/75.09, GRPO 52.55/75.55, GRPO-train 53.44/76.34. Teacher extractor: DeepSeek-V4-Flash.
limits: Small models (1.5B, 3B), one benchmark for the main table, EMNLP 2026 Findings. Single run per cell.
agent_relevance: Direct evidence for model dependence of a retrieved library (gap 8). Keep the library switchable per model.

source: Liu, Li, Dubrawski (2026) Notes to Self: where notes help and hurt (Table 6, Appendix A)
finding: The sign of the effect is predicted by how well the model already solves the problem. Injection helps problems the model mostly fails and hurts problems it already solves, more so after RL tuning. Internalisation is ruled out: plain GRPO, never trained with notes, is also hurt by injection.
numbers: Mean change in pass@1 by pre-injection per-problem accuracy bucket (500 MATH-500 problems): 0-50%: baseline +6.31, GRPO +3.62, GRPO-train +0.83. 50-100%: +2.46, -5.22, -3.61. Fully solved (100%): -2.32, -5.29, -1.12. OOD: helps OlympiadBench (weak), not GSM8K (saturated).
limits: Bucketing by pre-injection accuracy has regression-to-the-mean risk. The exploration-vs-sharpening explanation is not tested directly.
agent_relevance: A clean expertise-reversal analogue for LLMs (gap 1): give the hint only on items where the solver's own sample accuracy is low. Self-consistency over k samples can serve as the gate.

source: Liu, Li, Dubrawski (2026) Notes to Self: cross-model transfer and the Qwen failure (Table 4, Appendix B)
finding: Notes extracted from Llama traces were injected into other families. Gemma lost accuracy, even with a blank template. Qwen's loss came from broken answer format and a few badly matched retrievals (it followed a note for the opposite objective), not from caution notes acting as constraints.
numbers: MATH-500 pass@1/pass@8, baseline vs blank template vs notes: gemma-2-2B 21.77/43.00, 13.08/33.60, 13.75/33.40; gemma-3-3B 44.88/62.40, 42.02/62.40, 40.15/60.00; Phi-3.5-mini 40.62/64.00, 42.30/65.20, 43.60/65.80. One Qwen problem fell 50% to 16% after a mismatched note; one Llama problem rose 22% to 63% on a matched one.
limits: Case studies from one problem each. Table 4 read from PDF text.
agent_relevance: Answers gap 8: sign depends on (a) baseline strength on the item, (b) format fragility of the model, (c) retrieval fit. Log the format-failure rate before and after adding the library.

source: Zelikman, Wu, Mu, Goodman (2022) STaR: Bootstrapping Reasoning with Reasoning
finding: Self-written rationales are kept only if the final answer matches the gold answer (a verifier), then used to fine-tune. Rationalization (give the answer as a hint for failed items) adds solved items. Humans ranked STaR rationales above few-shot ones and above human ones.
numbers: Arithmetic: 2-digit addition from under 1% to 32% after one iteration; final arithmetic 89.5% vs 76.3% for a no-rationale baseline. GSM8K (GPT-J): few-shot CoT 3.1, direct fine-tune 5.8, STaR 10.1 (25.0% of data kept), with rationalization 10.7 (28.7%). Prolific ranking, 20 raters: STaR rationales preferred over few-shot by 30% (p=.039) and over human ones by 74% (p<.001).
limits: GPT-J 6B, weak base; an answer-only filter can keep wrong reasoning with a right answer. Fine-tuning, not in-context.
agent_relevance: Verifier-filtered self-made examples are a standard, working recipe (gaps 6 and 10). GSM8K gains at this scale are tiny, so do not over-read.

source: Search attempt: LLM studies of attempt-first vs example-first, fading by verified success, subgoal labels in natural-language maths
